\subsubsection{The transimpedance loop}

Closing the loop around the electrode changes the stability picture completely. The
amplifier has \SI{88}{\degree} of phase margin; the transimpedance loop built from it
peaks by \SIrange{5.0}{6.4}{\decibel} at about \SI{1}{\kilo\hertz}
(Figure~\ref{fig:tia-zt}). Nothing about the amplifier causes this.

Writing $C_{\mathrm{dl}}$ for the double-layer capacitance at the summing node, the
feedback factor and the closed-loop transimpedance are

\begin{equation}\label{eq:tia-beta}
  \beta(s) = \frac{1}{1 + s R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}}},
  \qquad
  Z_t(s) = \frac{V_{\mathrm{OUT}}}{I_{\mathrm{WE}}}
         = \frac{-R_f}{1 + \dfrac{1 + s R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}}}{A(s)}} .
\end{equation}

At DC the correction term is $1/A_0 = \num{6.1e-5}$, which is why the measured
transimpedance is within \SI{0.02}{\percent} of $R_f$. Above
$1/2\pi R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}} = \SI{0.28}{\hertz}$ the noise gain $1/\beta$ climbs at
\SI{20}{\decibel} per decade and meets the amplifier's own \SI{20}{\decibel}-per-decade
roll-off at

\begin{equation}\label{eq:tia-fx}
  f_x = \sqrt{\frac{f_u}{2 \pi R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}}}} \approx \SI{1.3}{\kilo\hertz},
\end{equation}

a \SI{40}{\decibel}-per-decade rate of closure. The measured peak sits at
\SIrange{1.00}{1.12}{\kilo\hertz}, so the \emph{frequency} of the resonance is
predicted well.

\paragraph{The magnitude is not.} Substituting the single-pole $A(s) = \omega_u/s$ into
Equation~(\ref{eq:tia-beta}) gives a second-order denominator with

\begin{equation}\label{eq:tia-q}
  \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{\omega_u}{R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}}}},
  \qquad
  Q = \sqrt{\omega_u R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}}} = \num{4700},
\end{equation}

which would be \SI{74}{\decibel} of peaking against the \SI{5.06}{\decibel} measured.
The discrepancy is not a small-signal detail: it says the ideal-op-amp TIA model does
not apply here. Its hidden assumption is that the amplifier drives the feedback network
from a zero output impedance, and this one does not --- $R_2 = \SI{737}{\kilo\ohm}$ is
larger than $R_f = \SI{560}{\kilo\ohm}$, so $R_f$ loads the output node it is fed from
and drops the available gain from \SI{84.4}{\decibel} to about \SI{77}{\decibel} before
the loop is even closed. \textbf{Quantifying this loop properly needs an \texttt{stb}
analysis through the existing \texttt{IPRB\_F} probe in \texttt{TiaFbTB}, which this run
does not contain} --- only \texttt{ac}. Until that is run, the peaking in
Figure~\ref{fig:tia-zt} is the measurement and the numbers above are only its mechanism.

\paragraph{Remedy.} The textbook fix is a feedback capacitor across $R_f$,
$C_f = \sqrt{C_{\mathrm{dl}} / (2 \pi R_f f_u)}$, which flattens the response and sets
the bandwidth to $1/2\pi R_f C_f$. At this gain setting that is of order
\SI{200}{\pico\farad} --- on the order of \SI{0.1}{\milli\metre\squared} of MIM per
channel, and four channels are needed. It is not an on-chip component at that size, and
because $C_f$ scales as $1/\sqrt{R_f}$ the requirement grows, not shrinks, at the lower
gain settings. Resolving this is the principal open item for the stage: the options are
an external capacitor on the WE pad, a deliberate reduction of $f_u$ (the amplifier has
\SI{88}{\degree} of margin to spend), or accepting the peaking and band-limiting after
the ADC. It should be settled before layout, since two of the three change the cell.

DC accuracy, by contrast, is not in question. Transimpedance at \SI{1}{\hertz} is within
\SI{0.02}{\percent} of $R_f$ at every corner, the incremental gain varies by
\SI{0.09}{\percent} across the current range, and the virtual ground holds to
\SI{0.4}{\milli\volt} --- under \SI{0.04}{\percent} of full scale. Below a few hundred
hertz the stage does exactly what it is specified to do.
